subject: 임상시험에서 동의가 뜻하는 것
title: What consent means in a medical trial
content: Before a person joins a trial they sign a form saying they understand the risks and agree to take part. The form protects the institution, and whether it does the moral work it claims to do is a separate question. Genuine consent requires understanding, voluntariness, and capacity, and each of these is harder to secure than the paperwork suggests. Understanding is the first difficulty. A patient told that a trial compares two treatments frequently believes the researchers know which is better and are offering them the better one. This misunderstanding is so common that it has a name, and it survives careful explanation, because a person who is ill hears whatever supports hope. A form signed under that belief records agreement to something other than what was described. Voluntariness is the second. Somebody whose doctor invites them into a study may feel that refusing would damage a relationship they depend upon, and somebody with no other access to a promising treatment has an alternative that is not really an alternative. Neither pressure is applied by anyone, and both are real. Justice requires attending to conditions rather than only to what was said. A further problem concerns what the participant is agreeing to. Trials change as they proceed, samples are stored and used for purposes nobody had thought of, and consent given once cannot cover research that did not exist. Broad permissions solve the administrative problem while emptying the moral one, since agreeing to unspecified future use is agreeing to nothing in particular. What follows is that consent is a process rather than a signature. Checking understanding afterwards, making refusal visibly costless, and returning for fresh agreement when the purpose changes are all available, and their absence reflects convenience rather than necessity. A form that records agreement without securing it protects everybody except the person it names.

subject: 세대 간 형평이라는 문제
title: Dividing what lasts longer than a lifetime
content: Some resources and some damages persist far beyond any human life. Deciding how much a present generation may use, and what condition it must leave things in, is a question of justice between people who will never meet and cannot bargain with one another. Ordinary moral tools handle it badly. The standard economic instrument discounts future costs, treating a harm arriving in a century as worth much less than the same harm today. There are respectable reasons for discounting when the question concerns money, since resources invested now yield more later. Applying the same rate to lives and to irreversible losses produces conclusions almost nobody accepts, since a modest rate makes catastrophes a few generations away nearly weightless. The choice of rate does more work than any other assumption in such calculations, and it is a moral choice presented as a technical one. A second difficulty concerns what is owed. One position holds that each generation should pass on capacities equivalent to what it received, allowing substitution: a forest lost is acceptable if knowledge gained is worth more. Another holds that certain things cannot be substituted, since no amount of built capital replaces a stable climate or an extinct kind. The disagreement is not about arithmetic but about whether value is fungible. A third difficulty is motivational rather than philosophical. Those who bear the cost of restraint are alive to complain, while those who benefit do not yet exist, and no political arrangement gives them a voice. Proposals for future guardians and long horizon institutions attempt to correct this, with limited success. What can be established is that the obligation is real even where its content is disputed. A generation that consumed everything and left the bill would have wronged somebody, and knowing that much is enough to reject the position that nothing is owed at all.

subject: 설득과 조작의 경계
title: Two ways of changing somebody's mind
content: Changing what another person believes or wants is an ordinary part of life, and most of it is entirely legitimate. Yet some methods strike us as wrongful even where the resulting belief is true and the outcome is good. Locating the difference is a genuine problem in moral philosophy, since both activities produce the same kind of result. The most promising account looks at how the change is produced. Persuasion offers a person reasons and leaves the assessment to them, so if they end up convinced it is because they judged the reasons adequate. Manipulation bypasses that judgment, working through emotion, timing, framing, or exhaustion, and its success does not depend on the reasons being any good. Consequently persuasion respects the person's rational agency while manipulation treats it as an obstacle. Two complications deserve attention. First, emotional appeal is not automatically manipulative, since some things genuinely warrant fear or indignation and pointing that out is legitimate. What matters is whether the emotion is fitting to the facts. Second, framing is unavoidable, because every presentation of information selects and orders, so the objection cannot be to framing itself but to framing chosen to defeat assessment rather than to enable it. A useful test asks about disclosure. If the target learned exactly what method was being used and would then feel resentment rather than gratitude, that is evidence of manipulation, whereas somebody shown a good argument does not resent having seen it. The test is not decisive and it is frequently illuminating. What the distinction protects is a value that outcomes cannot capture. Somebody manipulated into a true belief has been given something correct while being treated as a mechanism to be operated, and the moral wrong lies in that treatment rather than in any damage the belief does.

subject: 악숨의 비석과 홍해 교역
title: Stone pillars of a trading kingdom
content: In the highlands of what is now northern Ethiopia stand carved stone pillars, the largest of them over thirty metres and cut from a single block. They were raised by the kingdom of Aksum, a civilization that controlled the African side of the Red Sea trade during the first several centuries of our era, and they are among the largest single stones ever quarried and set upright anywhere. The carving on them imitates a building. Rows of beam ends, false doors, and window frames run up the face, so the pillar represents a tower of many storeys rendered in stone. They marked graves, and the largest belong to rulers, therefore the scale records both the wealth available and the ambition of the court that ordered them. The greatest of them appears to have fallen while being raised and lies broken where it landed. That wealth came from position. Aksum sat where goods from the interior of Africa, from India, and from the Mediterranean met, and its port handled ivory, gold, incense, and animals moving in several directions. The kingdom minted its own coinage in gold, silver, and bronze, which very few states of the era did, and the coins carry inscriptions in Greek as well as in the local script, indicating who the merchants were expected to be. The kingdom adopted Christianity in the fourth century, among the earliest states anywhere to do so, and the religious tradition established then has continued without interruption to the present. Later centuries brought decline as the trade routes shifted and the coast passed to others. What survives is a set of stones that puzzled European visitors for centuries, an unbroken church, and coins scattered across the region that allow historians to date a civilization whose own written records are thin.

subject: 노동조합과 집단의 힘
title: Why bargaining together is different
content: An individual worker negotiating with an employer holds a weak position, since the employer can replace them while they cannot easily replace their income. Bargaining collectively changes this, and the moral arguments about whether it should be permitted, encouraged, or restricted have run for two centuries without settling. The case for collective bargaining rests on correcting an asymmetry. Where one party can walk away and the other cannot, the resulting agreement reflects power rather than any judgment about what the work is worth. Combining removes that asymmetry without introducing coercion, since a group withholding labour is doing collectively what each member may do alone. On this reading a union restores the conditions under which an agreement means something. The case against has several forms. One holds that combination is itself a restraint on trade, and courts treated it as a criminal conspiracy for a long period on precisely that ground. Another holds that a union benefits its members at the expense of workers outside it, since higher wages for some may mean fewer positions overall. A third concerns compulsion within the group, where members who disagree with a decision are bound by it and those who decline to join may still receive the benefits. The internal question is genuinely difficult. Collective action works only if participation is high, so free riding threatens the whole arrangement, and yet requiring membership overrides individual choice. Different countries have settled this differently, and no arrangement satisfies everybody. What can be said is that the moral argument turns on the same principle that justifies contract generally. If agreements deserve respect because both parties chose them freely, then conditions that make one party's choice unfree matter, and an institution correcting those conditions is defending the value that contract was supposed to embody.

subject: 중세 수도원의 필사실
title: Rooms where books were copied by hand
content: Before printing, every book in Europe existed because somebody had written it out. Much of that work was done in monasteries, in rooms set aside for copying, and the arrangements developed there shaped which texts from the ancient world survived to be read in later centuries. This labour was severe. A scribe worked in daylight, since candles near parchment were forbidden, and their notes in the margins complain about aching fingers, poor light, and the length of the task. A substantial book might occupy one copyist for the better part of a year, and the materials were expensive as well, since a large volume required the skins of an entire herd. Such copies were therefore made only where somebody judged a text worth its cost. These judgments determined what survives. Works considered useful for worship, for law, or for teaching were copied repeatedly, while others were copied rarely or not at all, and a text that fell out of favour for a few generations could vanish entirely. Several ancient works are known to us through a single medieval copy, and their survival was an accident of one monastery's holdings. Errors accumulated throughout this process. A scribe misreading a word passed the mistake to every copy made from his, and later readers sometimes corrected the text by guessing, which produced further variants. Modern scholars reconstruct originals by comparing surviving manuscripts and reasoning about which errors are shared, since a common mistake indicates a common ancestor. Some houses developed careful practices to limit such damage, comparing their copy against the source and recording every correction. What the whole system illustrates is that transmission is never neutral. The ancient library that reached the medieval world had been filtered by a long sequence of decisions about what was worth a year of somebody's life.

subject: 민간인 면제는 왜 절대적인가
title: The rule that will not bend
content: Among the rules of war, the prohibition on deliberately attacking civilians is treated as admitting no exception. Other requirements yield to necessity in various ways, and this one is stated absolutely. Understanding why requires seeing what the rule is protecting and what would follow from allowing exceptions. One justification appeals to what makes anybody a legitimate target. On the standard account, combatants may be attacked because they pose a threat, and the permission tracks the threat rather than any judgment about guilt. Civilians pose no threat, therefore attacking them cannot be justified by the reasoning that justifies attacking anyone at all. The rule is not an exception carved out of a general permission; it marks where the permission stops. A second justification concerns what exceptions would do. The proposed exceptions always take the same form: attacking civilians would shorten the war and save lives overall. Historical cases show that this calculation is made confidently and turns out to be wrong, and that once it is available it expands, since any commander can construct the argument. A rule that yields to a sufficiently large expected benefit is not a rule but a presumption, and in war the estimates are made by the party who wants the exception. A third consideration concerns what remains after a war. Combatants who observed the limit can be reconciled with those they fought; a population that was deliberately targeted has a grievance that outlives every peace treaty. The rule therefore protects the possibility of ending a conflict rather than merely restraining it. What follows is that the absoluteness is doing real work. Stated as a strong presumption it would fail, because the cases where somebody wants to violate it are exactly the cases where they can construct a justification, and a limit that yields under pressure supplies no protection when pressure arrives.

subject: 전후 책임의 범위
title: What is owed when the fighting stops
content: Most moral discussion of war concerns whether to fight and how to fight, and considerably less attention has gone to what follows. Yet the period after a conflict determines whether the harm ends or continues, and the obligations arising then are neither obvious nor widely agreed. One position holds that a victor who fought justly owes nothing beyond ceasing hostilities. The war was justified, the aggression has been defeated, and demanding further contribution punishes those who did the right thing. This has some force, although it sits badly with the fact that the destruction was caused by the victor's own actions, however justified those actions were. A second position derives obligations from the aims that justified the war. If the fighting was justified as preventing a serious harm, then leaving conditions in which that harm returns defeats the justification retrospectively. On this reading reconstruction is not charity but completion, and abandoning a country to collapse means the original argument for intervening was never carried through. A third consideration concerns the population. Civilians in the defeated state did not choose the war, frequently opposed it, and suffered its consequences most, and treating them as liable for their government's decisions contradicts the very distinction that governed how the war was fought. Consequently postwar arrangements that impoverish an entire population are difficult to defend on the terms used to justify the fighting. The historical record supports the moral argument unusually clearly. Settlements imposing collective punishment have produced further conflict within a generation, while those investing in recovery have produced durable peace. That correlation is not proof, and the number of cases is small, although the mechanism is easy to state. What follows is that the obligation is real, expensive, and consistently underestimated when the decision to fight is being made.

subject: 대항해 시대의 해도 제작
title: Charts made by sailors who came back
content: The sea charts of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries were working documents rather than ornaments. They recorded coastlines, harbours, hazards, and the compass bearings between ports, and they were assembled from what returning crews reported. Their development is among the clearest cases in history of knowledge accumulating through many small contributions. The earlier tradition used a network of lines radiating from compass roses across the sheet. A navigator laid a straight edge between two ports, found the nearest matching line, and read off the bearing to steer, which worked adequately in an enclosed sea where distances were short. The method broke down on ocean crossings, since a constant compass bearing does not follow the shortest path on a sphere, and the error grows with distance. Charts were state property in several countries. Portugal and Spain treated their sailing directions as secrets, restricted copying, and punished those who sold information to rivals, because the knowledge of how to reach a coast was worth as much as the goods found there. Consequently much of what was learned during that era circulated slowly and by theft. The projection published in the sixteenth century that still bears its maker's name solved the navigational problem by distorting area, so that a constant bearing becomes a straight line on the sheet. Sailors gained a chart they could steer by, and every reader since has inherited a badly distorted picture of the relative size of the continents. Accumulation was the real achievement. Each voyage corrected a coastline, moved an island, or added a hazard, and the compilers in the port cities worked these reports into successive editions. A chart of that era is therefore not one person's work but a running record of everything that a great many crews had survived to report.

subject: 위법 수집 증거를 버리는 이유
title: Throwing away proof because of how it was obtained
content: A court that excludes reliable evidence because officials obtained it improperly appears to be defeating its own purpose. The material would have shown the truth, the accused may be guilty, and the rule may result in their release. Defending the practice therefore requires an argument, and several quite different ones are offered. The first is deterrence. Officials who know that improperly obtained material cannot be used lose the incentive to obtain it improperly, and no other sanction has proved effective. On this reading exclusion is a price paid to secure compliance, and its justification depends on whether it actually works, which is an empirical question with mixed answers. The second argument concerns the integrity of the court. A tribunal that convicts using material obtained by violating the accused's rights makes itself a participant in that violation, and the judgment it issues is tainted by the manner of its proof. This account does not depend on deterring anybody, since it concerns what the institution may do rather than what effects follow. The third argument appeals to the rights themselves. A protection against unlawful search is worth having only if breaching it costs something, and a right whose violation carries no consequence is a statement rather than a protection. Exclusion converts the right into an enforceable claim. The objections are serious. Guilty people are released, victims receive nothing, and the burden of the rule falls on the public rather than on the official who broke the rule. Several systems therefore admit exceptions where the breach was minor or made in good faith. What the debate makes clear is that the practice is not a technicality but a decision about the relative importance of convicting the guilty and constraining the state, and different societies have weighed those differently for reasons they can state.

subject: 즉흥 연주가 지키는 규칙
title: How improvisers know what to play
content: An audience hearing a performer invent music on the spot frequently assumes that anything may happen. Musicians in improvising traditions describe something quite different, since the freedom operates inside a dense set of constraints that everybody on the stand shares and nobody states aloud. The harmonic frame supplies the first constraint. A jazz performance ordinarily works through a repeating sequence of chords that every player knows, so the soloist's choices are heard against a structure the audience can follow even without naming it. Departing from the frame is available and expressive precisely because the frame exists, and a note that would be unremarkable in isolation carries weight when it contradicts what the harmony expects. Vocabulary supplies the second. Improvisers spend years absorbing phrases from recordings, and what they play is assembled from remembered material recombined rather than invented from nothing. This is not a deficiency, since the same is true of fluent speech, and the shared vocabulary is what allows the other musicians to anticipate and respond. A player quoting a phrase associated with a famous performance makes a reference the informed listener catches. The third constraint is social. An improvising group listens continuously, and a soloist who ignores what the drummer is doing has failed regardless of what they played. Musicians describe good improvisation as conversation, and the analogy is exact in an important respect: contributions are judged by their fit with what preceded them, not only by their own merits. What follows is that this art is closer to a language than to spontaneous expression. The freedom is real and it belongs to somebody who has spent a decade acquiring the constraints, which is why untrained playing sounds nothing like it and why the tradition takes teaching so seriously.

subject: 조몬 토기의 편년
title: Dating a culture by its pots
content: The Jomon culture of the Japanese islands produced pottery for roughly ten thousand years, which makes it among the longest continuous ceramic traditions anywhere. Its vessels are known for elaborate rims and cord-marked surfaces, and the name of the ancient culture itself refers to the cord impressions. For archaeologists the pottery has served a further purpose. Because styles changed steadily and the changes were regional, the sequence of forms functions as a clock. A fragment recovered from a site can be assigned to a phase, and the phase places the layer in time without any laboratory work. Generations of researchers built this framework by excavating stratified deposits where later styles lay above earlier ones, and the resulting chronology divides the era into a long series of named phases. Radiocarbon dating, when it arrived, produced a surprise. The earliest pottery from these islands turned out to be far older than anybody had expected, older than agriculture anywhere, which contradicted the assumption that ceramics accompany farming. Pots were being made by people who hunted, fished, and gathered, and the vessels were apparently used for cooking nuts and marine foods rather than for storing grain. Residue analysis has since confirmed what was cooked in some of them. The tradition's stability is the deeper puzzle. Ten thousand years of continuity, with elaboration rather than replacement, suggests a way of life that met its needs and had no reason to change. Settlements were substantial, populations were considerable in some regions, and the eventual transition came from outside rather than from within. What the pottery finally supplies is a rare fine-grained record of an ancient culture that left no writing. The vessels record contact between regions, shifts in cooking, and the timing of change, and almost everything known about the sequence rests on them.

subject: 재범 예측과 선고
title: Sentencing somebody for what they might do
content: Courts increasingly consult statistical estimates of whether an offender will commit a further offence, and the estimates influence release and sentence length. The practice is defended as replacing intuition with evidence, and it raises moral questions that the improvement in accuracy does not answer. The first concerns what a sentence is for. If punishment responds to what somebody did, then adding time because of what they might do punishes an act that has not occurred. Preventive detention of that kind is defensible only on a different theory, in which the state may restrain dangerous people regardless of desert, and most legal systems reject that theory when it is stated openly while applying it through the back door. The second concerns the inputs. Predictors include employment, housing stability, family circumstances, and prior contact with the system, and these correlate with poverty and with which communities were policed heavily. An offender therefore receives a longer sentence partly because of conditions they did not choose and that the state helped produce. Calling the result objective conceals the inheritance. The third concerns the individual. A statistical estimate describes a group, and applying it to a person treats them as a representative of that group rather than as themselves. Where the estimate is wrong, the person has no way to demonstrate it in advance, since the prediction concerns conduct that will not occur. Defenders reply that judges predicted anyway, less accurately and with their own biases, so the comparison is not between a model and pure justice. This is a serious point. What it supports is a narrow use with strong safeguards, and what it cannot support is presenting such numbers to a court as though they described the person standing there.

subject: 만화의 칸과 시간
title: How panels make time pass
content: Comics tell stories through images arranged in sequence, and the reader supplies everything that happens between them. A figure raises an arm in one panel and the blow has landed in the next, so the action itself was never drawn. This gap is where the art actually operates, and cartoonists have developed a detailed craft around controlling it. The width of a gap determines how much time passes. Two panels showing nearly identical images read as a moment, while panels separated by a change of location read as hours or years, and the reader adjusts without instruction. Consequently a page can compress a decade or expand a second, and the choice is made by how much difference the artist places between adjacent images. Panel size and shape reinforce the effect. A wide panel is read slowly because the eye travels further across it, and a sequence of narrow panels produces a staccato rhythm. A single image occupying a full page halts the reading entirely, which is why such pages are reserved for moments meant to arrest. These are physical facts about how eyes move, converted into an aesthetic vocabulary. The page as a whole is seen before it is read. A reader takes in the arrangement peripherally, so a shape at the bottom of the page is faintly known while the top is being read, and cartoonists either exploit this or design against it. Traditions differ in how much they care, and comics published in serialised form handle the page turn as a deliberate device. What the medium demonstrates is an art built on inference. Nothing on the paper moves, no duration is specified, and yet readers experience pacing as precisely as in film, because the tradition has worked out which arrangements produce which sensations of time.

subject: 무대 의상과 인물의 압축
title: Clothing that tells you who somebody is
content: A costume designer must convey a great deal before the character speaks. The audience sees the figure from a distance, in changing light, for a few seconds before the scene begins, and whatever they conclude will colour everything that follows. The craft consists in packing information into that first impression. Silhouette carries most of it. Shape is legible from the back of a theatre where detail is not, so designers work first on the outline, and a character's outline frequently changes across a production to register what has happened to them. A figure who begins in stiff structured clothing and ends in something loose has been described without a word. Colour operates as a system rather than as decoration. Designers assign families of colour to groups so that alliances and divisions are visible at a glance, and a character who crosses between groups may carry a detail from the other side long before the plot acknowledges it. Audiences read these relationships without noticing that they are doing so. Historical accuracy is a genuine question rather than an obvious virtue. A production set in an earlier era may dress its characters exactly as the period did, which risks the audience reading the clothing as costume rather than as character, or it may borrow selectively so that modern viewers receive the impression the original clothing gave to its contemporaries. Both approaches are defensible and they cannot be combined. The constraint that shapes everything is the performer's body. A costume must permit whatever the staging demands, survive eight performances a week, and be changed quickly in the dark. Designers describe the art as a negotiation between what an image requires and what a moving person can wear, and the tradition values solutions that serve both.

subject: 도덕 판단은 감정의 표현인가
title: Whether moral talk states facts at all
content: When somebody says that cruelty is wrong, they appear to be describing something. The sentence has the same form as a factual claim, it can be argued about, and it seems capable of being true. One influential position in moral philosophy denies all of this, holding that such utterances express attitudes rather than state facts. The motivation for the position is genuine. Moral properties fit awkwardly into an account of the world built from physical description, since nothing observable corresponds to wrongness. Moreover moral judgments seem connected to motivation in a way that ordinary beliefs are not: somebody who sincerely judges an act wrong is thereby disposed against it, whereas believing that a wall is white disposes them toward nothing. Treating the judgment as an attitude explains both features at once. The difficulties appear when the position tries to accommodate ordinary moral reasoning. We embed moral claims in conditionals — if lying is wrong then encouraging it is wrong — and such arguments appear valid. If the claims express attitudes rather than propositions, explaining why the inference works becomes surprisingly hard, and a great deal of subsequent work has gone into solving exactly this problem. A further difficulty concerns disagreement. Two people arguing about whether a practice is wrong behave as though one of them is mistaken, and describing this as a clash of attitudes seems to miss what they take themselves to be doing. Sophisticated versions of the position accommodate much of this by treating moral discourse as a practice with its own standards of correctness, which brings it closer to the realist accounts it was opposing. What survives the exchange is a sharper question. Whatever moral judgments are, they must both connect to motivation and support argument, and any theory that secures one while losing the other has not yet described the practice we actually have.

subject: 장례 의례의 미학
title: The forms that a culture gives to death
content: Every culture surrounds death with prescribed forms: what is worn, what is said, how the body is treated, how long the observance lasts. These arrangements differ enormously and they are never arbitrary, since each encodes an understanding of what has happened and what the living owe the dead. Reading them as aesthetic traditions is illuminating. Colour is the most visible variable. Black in one tradition, white in another, and specific combinations elsewhere mark the mourner, and the marking serves a practical function as well as an expressive one, since it tells everybody they meet how to behave toward them. Traditions that have abandoned distinctive mourning dress frequently report a difficulty that the older arrangement solved, because a grieving person now moves through ordinary life without any signal. Duration is prescribed with equal care. Many traditions specify a sequence of stages with different requirements at each, and the sequence gives the mourner a structure to move through when their own judgment is unreliable. Anthropologists have noted that such stages frequently correspond to the practical course of grief, which suggests the forms were shaped by long observation rather than by doctrine alone. Sound and silence are handled deliberately. Some traditions require loud and public lament, performed by specialists in certain cultures, while others prize restraint and treat display as improper. Neither is more natural, and members of each frequently find the other disturbing, which is a useful reminder that these responses feel spontaneous while being learned. What such traditions supply is a form to occupy when nothing feels possible. The instructions are precise, they require no decisions, and following them connects the mourner to everybody who followed them before. Cultures that have thinned their observances have made the occasion a matter of individual invention, and the reported difficulty of that is evidence about what the old forms were doing.

subject: 자수와 이름 없는 손
title: Needlework and the makers nobody recorded
content: Embroidered cloth survives in huge amounts from many cultures, and almost none of it carries a maker's name. The work was done mostly by women, often at home rather than in shops, and the tradition that built museum collections had no box for fine things made by unknown hands. That view has been slow to change, and it is changing now. The demands of the craft are severe. A large piece may hold hundreds of thousands of stitches, needs a plan that cannot be changed once begun, and rests on judgments about tension and slant that decide how light falls on the finished face. Those who do it say the skill takes many years, and the gap between sound work and fine work is plain to anybody who has tried it and unseen by most who have not. Some famous survivals record history directly. A long embroidered hanging made in the eleventh century narrates an invasion across seventy metres, and it is among the principal sources for the events it depicts, consulted by historians for details of ships, weapons, and dress found nowhere else. The people who executed it are unknown, while the events they recorded are studied continuously. Domestic work carries different information. Samplers made by girls learning the craft record alphabets, ages, and occasionally complaints, and taken together they document education and household life across centuries in a form no written source supplies. Sets of such pieces have become sources for social history rather than mere displays of skill. What has changed is the label. Work once filed as craft is now shown as art, and the shift matters because the old label decided what was bought, kept, and studied. A great deal was thrown out before the change, which is the usual cost of a ranking that nobody looked at.

subject: 신석기 농경의 확산 경로
title: How farming travelled across a continent
content: Agriculture began in a small number of places and spread from them, and tracing the spread across Europe has occupied archaeologists for over a century. The crops and animals involved were domesticated in the Near East, and they appear across the continent over roughly three thousand years, moving broadly from the south east toward the north west. Two explanations competed for a long period. One held that farming spread as a technique, learned by hunting and gathering populations who adopted it from their neighbours. The other held that farmers themselves moved, expanding gradually into new ground and absorbing or displacing those already there. The distinction matters, since one describes the transmission of an idea and the other a movement of people. Ancient genomes have largely settled it. The earliest farming populations in Europe carry ancestry closely related to populations in the Near East, which indicates migration rather than adoption alone. Yet the picture is not simple replacement, since hunter gatherer ancestry persists and in some regions increases again in later centuries, showing that the two populations mixed over a long period rather than one simply erasing the other. The pace was uneven. Expansion moved rapidly along the river valleys of central Europe and along the Mediterranean coast, then paused for centuries at certain frontiers before continuing. Those pauses correspond to environments where the imported crops did badly, therefore the spread was constrained by what would grow rather than by any resistance from people. What the case demonstrates is how much a single question can be transformed by new evidence. A debate conducted for decades on the basis of pottery styles and settlement patterns was resolved by material nobody had known was recoverable, and the resolution turned out to include a substantial part of both original positions.

subject: 재즈의 대화 구조
title: Musicians answering one another
content: A jazz performance is often described as a conversation, and this description is more precise than most musical metaphors. The players are responding to one another continuously, and much of what an informed listener attends to is not the melody but the exchange taking place beneath it. Because the exchange is continuous, the rhythm section carries most of it. A drummer hearing a soloist build tension will increase density and volume, a bassist may move from a walking line into something sparser to open space, and a pianist may stop playing entirely to let a phrase stand alone. None of this is written, and it changes from one night to the next, so recordings of the same group playing the same piece differ substantially, although the tune is identical. Certain structures make this exchange explicit. Trading passages in which soloist and drummer alternate short phrases turn the conversation into the form itself, and the second player is expected to answer what the first just did rather than to play something prepared. Audiences familiar with this tradition listen for exactly that relation, and they can tell when it fails. Because this tradition values responsiveness so highly, several of its judgments puzzle outsiders. A technically brilliant solo that ignored the band may be dismissed, while a simpler contribution that answered what was happening is praised, because the tradition values the interaction above individual display. Musicians speak of players who listen as the highest compliment available. What these habits reveal is a form of collective authorship. No single person composed what the audience hears, the material was shaped by everybody present including the audience whose response the players register, and the piece exists only in that performance. Few arts distribute the making so widely, and the tradition's insistence on live performance follows directly from what it values.

subject: 도덕 판단과 행위 동기
title: Why knowing what is right seems to move us
content: There appears to be a connection between judging that an act is right and being disposed to perform it. Somebody who sincerely holds that they ought to help and feels no inclination whatever strikes us as puzzling, in a way that somebody who believes it will rain without caring does not. Explaining this connection has divided moral philosophy for a long period. One position holds that the connection is necessary. Moral judgments are not ordinary beliefs; they include or entail a motivational state, which is why sincerity and indifference cannot coexist. This explains the phenomenon directly, although it commits the position to saying that a person entirely unmoved was not really judging, which strains against cases where somebody appears to know exactly what they should do while doing nothing. The opposing position holds that the connection is contingent. Moral judgments are beliefs about how things are, and beliefs move us only in combination with desires, so a person indifferent to morality would be strange without being incoherent. This account handles the difficult cases comfortably. Its cost is that it makes the ordinary connection a matter of most people happening to care, which seems to understate how deep the link runs. A middle position distinguishes normal from defective cases. Moral judgment is connected to motivation in the way that vision is connected to seeing: reliably, and defeasibly under conditions of depression, exhaustion, or despair. On this reading somebody unmoved is not a counterexample but a case of the mechanism failing. The debate has practical relevance for how we treat wrongdoing. If moral knowledge normally motivates, then somebody who acted badly either did not see clearly or was impaired, and the responses appropriate to those two conditions differ enormously from each other and from simple blame.

subject: 희극과 비극의 사회적 기능
title: Why cultures keep both kinds of play
content: Dramatic traditions across many cultures maintain a division between works ending badly and works ending well, and the division is not merely a matter of mood. Each form does something the other cannot, and cultures that possess theatre almost always possess both. Tragedy presents a serious person destroyed by something they could not entirely avoid. Ancient accounts of its effect describe the arousal and release of pity and fear, and later theories emphasise that the form allows an audience to look at what they ordinarily avoid. Watching a fall from a safe seat is not the same as suffering it, and the tradition holds that this rehearsal is valuable rather than merely morbid. What tragedy insists upon is that some situations have no acceptable exit. Comedy inverts the machinery. Its characters are ordinary or worse, their errors produce confusion rather than catastrophe, and the ending restores order. The form permits attacks on authority that would be intolerable stated directly, since a joke can be disowned, and the licensed mockery of powerful figures appears in comic traditions across unconnected cultures. Where tragedy asks the audience to accept limits, comedy asks them to notice that arrangements presented as necessary are frequently absurd. The social functions are correspondingly different. A culture with only tragedy would present its structures as fate; one with only comedy would present nothing as serious. Holding both allows a society to say simultaneously that suffering is real and that authority is ridiculous, and neither statement alone would be adequate. The forms have never been entirely separate. Many of the strongest works mix them, placing comic material inside a tragic structure to sharpen it, and audiences accept the mixture readily. What the traditions preserve is not two boxes but two directions of attention, both of which a culture apparently needs.

subject: 수집과 분류 — 진열장의 논리
title: The cabinet and what it argues
content: Before museums existed in the modern sense, wealthy collectors assembled cabinets holding whatever struck them as remarkable: shells, coins, carvings, fossils, instruments, and objects from distant places. Such collections look chaotic to modern eyes, and their arrangement followed a logic that repays attention. The cabinet was organised by wonder rather than by category. A carved cup stood beside a stone that resembled a face, and both were present because they provoked the same response, so the collection asserted that art and nature were continuous rather than opposed. This was a claim about the world, made through arrangement rather than through argument, and visitors understood it as such. The later separation into museums of art, of natural history, and of ethnography imposed a different claim. Objects were sorted by what kind of thing they were, and the sorting embodied a view in which nature, art, and other cultures occupy distinct categories requiring distinct expertise. A carved figure that had stood beside a shell now stood beside other carved figures, and its meaning changed accordingly. The classification was not discovered; it was applied. The consequences for objects taken from other societies were considerable. Placed in a natural history collection, such works were presented as specimens of a people rather than as art by individuals, and the framing persisted for a century. Recent reinstallations moving them into art galleries make a different claim, and the debate about which framing is correct is genuinely unresolved. What any display argues is therefore worth reading deliberately. A case grouping objects by material asserts that material matters; one grouping by region asserts that place does. Visitors absorb the assertion without noticing it, which is precisely why curators regard the arrangement as the substance of their work rather than as its packaging.

subject: 기념 조형물과 집단 기억
title: What a monument asks a city to remember
content: A monument fixes a judgment in durable material and places it where people must pass. Its purpose is to make remembering unnecessary, since the object remembers on the community's behalf, and this delegation is exactly what makes such works contested long after they are built. The traditional form was the figure on a pedestal. Raising somebody above eye level and casting them in bronze asserts that they were admirable and that the matter is settled, and the visual language leaves no room for qualification. Consequently disputes about such works become disputes about whether to keep or remove, since the form itself admits no third option. Twentieth century practice moved in a different direction. Memorials to catastrophe frequently avoid figures entirely, using names, voids, or shapes that resist interpretation, and this shift responds to a judgment that certain events cannot be represented by a heroic image without falsifying them. A wall of names asks the visitor to find one, which converts remembering from something the object does into something the visitor performs. The reception of such works has been instructive. Several were criticised bitterly when proposed, on the ground that they refused the consolation a monument was supposed to supply, and several are now among the most visited memorials anywhere. The audience learned a new form, which took roughly a generation. Recent practice has added a further option: leaving a contested work in place while adding material that reframes it. This produces an object that records both the original judgment and the later reconsideration, which is arguably a truer account than either the untouched monument or the empty plinth. Whether a city wants its public spaces to display that kind of argument is itself a question about what public memory is for.
